agenda you would like to speak on and will unmute your mic at the appropriate time.

Agenda reports and other disclosable public records relating to each agenda item are available on the City's
website under Meeting Agendas, Minutes & Videos at www.rhe.city/agendas.

MINUTES
  GENERAL PLAN ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  SEPTEMBER 15, 2020

1.  CHAIR SCHMITZ called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m.

2.  ROLL CALL

  COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT:  Schmitz, Addleman, Arata, Bayer, Buresh,
  Carman, Corman, Medawar, Seamans,
  Shinn, Stegura, Zuckerman

  COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT:  Carrese, Silvano

  STUDENT MEMBERS PRESENT:  Scandaliato, Wagreich

  STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT:  Greg Grammer, City Manager
  David Wahba, Director of Community Development
  and Public Works
  Jeannie Naughton, Planning Manager
  Kelley Thom, Associate Planner
  Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant

  ALSO PRESENT:  John Bellas, Principal, Michael Baker International
  Surabhi Barbhaya, Senior Planner, Michael Baker International
  Amanda Chapman, Internal Project Manager, Fehr & Peers
  Seth Contreras, Project Planner, Fehr & Peers
  John Muggridge, Principal, Fehr & Peers

3.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

A.  APPROVAL OF GENERAL PLAN ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES,
  JUNE 30, 2020.

COMMITTEE MEMBER MEDAWAR made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
CARMAN to,

  APPROVE THE GENERAL PLAN ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES OF
  JUNE 30, 2020.

There being no objection, CHAIR SCHMITZ so ordered.

4.  AUDIENCE ITEMS WRITTEN/ORAL COMMUNICATIONS NOT ON AGENDA

NONE

5.  DISCUSSION ITEMS

A.  MOBILITY ELEMENT

John Bellas, Principal, Michael Baker International (MBI), introduced the consultants from Fehr &
Peers, who will be providing a presentation on the Mobility Element.

Amanda Chapman, Internal Project Manager, Fehr and Peers provided a brief outline of the
meeting including the purpose of the Mobility Element, which addresses the transportation system
in the City. The process will be to identify what is working well and what can be improved and
provide a framework to address the issues and create a plan on how to implement improvements.

John Muggridge, Principal, Fehr and Peers, provided a presentation on transportation analysis
measures. Mr. Muggridge provided a brief overview of SB743, which is an update on how
transportation impacts of proposed development and plans are measured under CEQA. Prior to
SB743 driver impacts were measured using Level of Services (LOS); after SB743 driver impacts
are measured using Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT). The State had three main goals for going from
LOS to VMT, including, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging infill development, and

 GENERAL PLAN ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  1
 MINUTES, SEPTEMBER 15, 2020
 improving public health through increased active transportation (walking and biking). The new
criteria aims to promote the development of multimodal transportation networks, increase diversity
of land uses, and ensure that environmental impacts of traffic continue to be addressed through
CEQA. Mr. Muggridge explained that LOS mitigation measures added capacity allowing people
to travel more; VMT mitigation strategies focus on reducing VMT and this is known as
Transporation Demand Management. A brief overview on these strategies were presented
including; telecommuting, increase mixed use development, commute trip reduction programs,
parking management, provide pedestrian network improvements, bicycle and traffic calming
networks, implement car sharing and ride sharing programs, and increase transit accessibility.
Mr. Muggridge provided other metrics that can be used, including but not limited to: LOS, vehicle
trips, mode split, and distance to active transportation infrastructure.

Seth Contreras, Project Planner, Fehr and Peers, provided a presentation on existing conditions,
and noted that the data that will be presented is from 2017, prior to COVID-19. The data for work
trips confirms that Rolling Hills Estates is a car dependent city and this is due to the land use,
which is mainly residential and low density, and the terrain. The data also shows that 10% of
residents work from home and expect this number to be higher now. Mr. Contreras provided an
overview of commuter flow, including where residents are travelling for work, and where workers
into the City commute from. A vehicle collision summary was presented to highlight safety
concerns that have been raised in previous surveys. The data shows that the VMT in the City is
higher than the regional average. The intersection LOS data shows that the City has 16
intersections that were analyzed in 2017 and the majority of intersections have good operations.
Most of the congestion is concentrated on PVDN in the PM peak hour. Mr. Contreras stated that
the key findings are, 1) congestion is limited, yet concentrated; 2) the car is the predominant mode
of transportation; 3) addressing bicycle networking gaps and take into consideration the change
in grade and safety concerns; and, 4) looking at the SCAG 2016 Regional Transportation Plan,
which is soon to be updated.

Ms. Chapman provided an overview on previous public engagement comments that were
provided, which will be taken into account going forward. Most of the concerns were in regards to
transportation, some of which include, improving congestion, making it safer to walk, making it
easier to take public transportation, and improving transportation options for seniors.

Prior to the meeting, the GPAC was asked to complete a survey, which included the following
questions:

  •  Which elements of the transportation network do you think need the most focus? Consider
  your top priorities.
  •  Have you seen anything in another jurisdiction that you’d like to see in Rolling Hills
  Estates? Consider BOTH policy or physical implementation of a project.
  •  Where could you see more opportunities for biking, walking or other active modes?
  •  Thinking creatively, please share any other ideas for the future of mobility in Rolling Hills
  Estates.

Q.1. Which elements of the transportation network do you think need the most focus? Consider
your top priorities.

The walking network and specific streets received the most votes. Specific streets include Deep
Valley Drive and Palos Verdes Drive North (PVDN). Specific intersections mentioned include:
PVDN/Crenshaw, PVDN/Hawthorne, Crenshaw/Highridge, Hawthorne/Silver Spur, and
Crenshaw/Silver Spur. Specific places mentioned were connectivity in and to the commercial
district. Additional areas of focus include: focus on environment, using and promoting public
transportation, consider a transit loop around the Commercial Business District (CBD) to connect
many amenities, dedicated safe walking routes, solutions for school-related traffic, car-pooling,
and Uber/Lyft drop-off zones in the CBD.

COMMITTEE MEMBER ADDLEMAN stated that the City does not have a bus and transit network,
so a walking network is important. An important network to consider is a biking network and it
would be interesting to consider locking racks in both the Promenade and Peninsula Center. Mr.
Addleman commented that the transit loop around the CBD did not work.

In response to a question by Ms. Chapman, COMMITTEE MEMBER ADDLEMAN stated that
either the standard bike rack or bike lockers could be considered. In addition, bike sharing may
also be considered.

 GENERAL PLAN ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  2
 MINUTES, SEPTEMBER 15, 2020
 In response to a question by Mr. Bellas, COMMITTEE MEMBER ADDLEMAN stated that the
transit loop was tried during the holiday period for three years and there were no riders and it
does not work.

In response to a question by Ms. Barbhaya, COMMITTEE MEMBER ADDLEMAN stated that this
was attemped between 2010 and 2015.

COMMITTEE MEMBER FRIEDMAN stated that she encourages pedestrian travel and would like
to see a transportation overlay zone for the Peninsula Center. Specifically, she stated her
concerns about Deep Valley Drive, which was designed to be a local street to serve the local
merchants and the collective street was supposed to be Silver Spur Road. People who live there,
have stated that Deep Valley Drive has been used as a short cut since there are no lights. Many
residents walk and would like to walk to local services and Deep Valley Drive is not conducive to
walking. Ms. Friedman stated that many projects did not take into consideration encouraging safe
walkability on Deep Valley Drive.

COMMITTEE MEMBER ZUCKERMAN stated that VMT does not measure congestion. Although
LOS cannot be used for environmental review purposes, City planners and the community may
like to know about different alternatives with respect to projects and transportation changes.

COMMITTEE MEMBER ZUCKERMAN asked, in regards to VMT, what is the threshold. Mr.
Muggridge stated that the State has come up with guidance, for VMT per capita or VMT per
employment. What is stated in the guidance is that you have the ability to set your threshold.
Suggestions given are a regional or citywide average. The earlier presentation showed VMT per
capita and VMT per employment for the SCAG region and compared it to the whole region. There
are many metrics to measure VMT and during this process, a few options will be presented and
will work through establishing thresholds.

COMMITTEE MEMBER ZUCKERMAN expressed his concern with reducing parking supply. He
stated that a statewide solution that could be applied to this City should be discussed. Mr.
Muggridge stated that it is a good metric in certain circumstances, so it is important to hear what
the committee thinks about parking.

Ms. Chapman stated that not all strategies are going to work for every communities and different
strategies will be used in different ways.

COMMITTEE MEMBER ZUCKERMAN suggested a metric that the City of Irvine uses. The city
has drawn a boundary around the Irvine Business Center and done a Capacity Analysis that may
be useful in this community. Mr. Muggridge stated that this could be explored.

Mr. Muggridge stated that in regards to LOS, it can still be looked at and there are different ways
to apply it.

COMMITTEE MEMBER SEAMANS stated that she is not sure that attention is being paid to how
small the City is and how local businesses operate. Ms. Seamans expressed her concern with
planning for the next 20 years at this time and stated that the population is key. There are many
elderly in the City. Another aspect to think about is the cost to repair and widen streets. Ms.
Seamans also stated that parking should remain as is.

Mr. Bellas stated that now is the time to think about what the community wants and there may be
ways to fund them.

COMMITTEE MEMBER ARATA asked if there was ever a study on who was riding the local bus.
He also commented that he agrees that bikes are a viable alternative and now that electric bikes
are becoming more popular, especially with students, the provision of bike parking/charging
stations should be explored.

CHAIR SCHMITZ stated that the City Council rotates and sits on the Board of PV Transit and
stated that PV Transit does a ridership study. The schedules depend on ridership.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAYER suggested that more crosswalks are needed to make crossing
safe. Encouraging the walking schoolbus would be helpful. There are many neighborhoods that
do not have sidewalks and recommended encouraging sidewalks for safety reasons. Ms. Bayer

 stated that she would like to find ways to encourage more community involvement from younger
people.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BURESH stated that she has a unique perspective since she used to
drive to downtown Los Angeles to work and now has an office on this hill. The topography and
age trends makes walking a difficult option. Ms. Buresh expressed her concern with traffic on
Rolling Hills Road.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BURESH stated that as a parent and a PTA member, there have been
many attempts to encourage children walking to school. However, it seems to be more difficult for
the parents since many are dropping off their children and going to work. School traffic is a big
part of the problem and this should be a priority. Enforcing rules already in place may also be
helpful.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BURESH stated that most people are biking for recreation and with the
topography, she is not sure how much of an option this actually is. Ms. Chapman stated that while
she was in the City, she agrees that most people are recreational bikers.

COMMITTEE MEMBER CORMAN stated that congestion on PVDN between Hawthorne Blvd. to
Rolling Hills Road is something that should be addressed. Due to the topography and hills, walking
and biking should be taken off the table. There is an opportunity to improve walkways and
crosswalks in the commercial district and making it more of a destination.

Mr. Muggridge stated that they are very familiar with the type of topography in the City. They
recently worked on the General Plan for the City of Diamond Bar, which has a very similar
topography. Mr. Muggridge assured the committee that they will be very careful on suggestions
of where to put the bicycle network and bicycle facilities.

COMMITTEE MEMBER CARMAN stated that school traffic is a big problem not only for the
residents but for the people who are employed here. The presentation showed the OC Van on
Demand and MicroVans, which may be an alternative to transport students. She agrees with
adding more crosswalks and making safe intersections. Carpool sign-up to various schools may
also be helpful.

COMMITTEE MEMBER MEDAWAR suggested an electric trolley system in the business district
that can be funded by SCE or the local merchants. Other cities have had success with this
approach.

COMMITTEE MEMBER STEGURA stated that the bike share idea is interesting and suggested
that if PV Transit, does not already have this, to have bike racks on their buses. However, bike
areas have to be safe to ride. PV Transit is mostly used by students and should consider
expanding the loop. Ms. Stegura suggested roundabouts and can be placed in different areas of
the commercial district.

STUDENT MEMBER WAGREICH stated that if VMT is the main metric, it may ignore things that
exist in PV. This is a distant City and the VMT would be large, but many have fuel efficient cars
that make the carbon footprint relatively lower than in other more concentrated cities that have a
worse level of service.

STUDENT MEMBER SCANDALIATO agreed that improving congestion on PVDN from
Hawthorne to Rolling Hills Road. Also, informing more parents about the walking schoolbus and
making it feasible for parents and students.

CHAIR SCHMITZ thanked the committee for their input. One of the overarching themes is that
there is a desire to solve these problems. The way that residents get home from work/school is
different from how residents mobilize once they get home and go shopping or get services. There
are a variety of way that could work and hope that all of this is being taken into consideration.

MS. CHAPMAN stated that this City is unique and would hope to tailor the suggestions to the
needs of the residents.

COMMITTEE MEMBER SHINN stated that it would be wonderful to go up the hills, but not people
could do this. Electric bikes will probably have a place in the community. The bus that goes around
the hill and drop off zones for Uber are great ideas. Most retail will be done online and not sure if

 GENERAL PLAN ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  4
 MINUTES, SEPTEMBER 15, 2020
 there will be a lot of retail in the City. The business district with gathering places, restaurants, and
walking paths may be something to look into. Ms. Shinn stated that she is not in favor of putting
sidewalks in the neighborhoods.

Ms. Chapman went over the remaining survey questions.

Have you seen anything in another jurisdiction that you’d like to see in Rolling Hills Estates?
Consider BOTH policy or physical implementation of a project.

Responses were equally divided between yes and no. Suggestions have already been discussed.

Where could you see more opportunities for biking, walking or other active modes?

Two things specifically, the mostly highly desired pedestrian area is along the commercial corridor
and the possibility of connecting people via active modes to schools in the area.

Thinking creatively, please share any other ideas for the future of mobility in Rolling Hills Estates.

The responses to this questions showed that it is very clear that there is a desire to promote a
sense of place and community.

CHAIR SCHMITZ stated that the last mile traveled needs to be something that residents are able
to walk. The idea of a green path could be something to consider. The idea of ride sharing is
good, but it may not make sense for vendors to have a presence in this City. Although residents
may prefer to drive to the commercial center, once they get there, the way they get around may
be different.

COMMITTEE MEMBER ZUCKERMAN stated that the idea of creating a promenade is important
and one place could be Silver Spur. Also, using Deep Valley Drive to Peninsula Shopping Center
and somehow getting across Norris Center Drive either walking or in a vehicle.

6.  CONSULTANT/STAFF/COMMITTEE ITEMS

Mr. Bellas provided last comments and next steps. Ms. Champan thanked everyone for their
participation and input. Mr. Muggridge thanked everyone as well.

7.  ADJOURNMENT

CHAIR SCHMITZ thanked the committee and adjourned the meeting at 7:52 p.m.

Respectfully submitted,  Approved by,

______________________________  _____________________________
Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant  Velveth Schmitz, Chair
